## Birdwatching Tourism: An Economic Engine for Motril

Dawn catches a group of British birdwatchers by surprise, binoculars resting on the railing of the main observation point. They have traveled from Norfolk, one of the meccas of European birdwatching, to note in their field notebooks the presence of the purple swamphen and the black-crowned night heron, two of the species that make the Charca de Suárez a mandatory stop for ornithology enthusiasts. They are no exception: every year, more than 20,000 people visit this Motril wetland, and approximately 30% of them arrive from the United Kingdom, Germany, and the Netherlands with a clear objective and a list of birds to spot.

Birdwatching tourism has ceased to be a marginal activity and has become a segment with significant weight within the local economy. A study conducted by the University of Granada puts the average daily expenditure of these visitors at 80 euros, an amount distributed among accommodations, restaurants, shops, and specialized guide services. The figure gains greater relevance considering that the birdwatcher profile tends to extend their stay over several days, travel during the low season, and prioritize destinations with well-preserved natural heritage—three characteristics that align with the offering Motril has begun to develop around its wetland.

The municipal strategy has not been limited to waiting for tourists to arrive by chance. The Motril City Council has signed collaboration agreements with travel agencies specialized in nature, a step that allows the Charca de Suárez to be included in tour packages that visit other Andalusian sites such as Doñana, the Strait of Gibraltar, or the Alpujarras. These agreements guarantee a steady flow of organized visitors while positioning the wetland within international nature tourism circuits, a market that moves millions of travelers each year in Europe.

The presence of the Charca de Suárez at international fairs has been another pillar of this international projection. The Motril council has attended BirdFair, the most important ornithology fair in the world, held annually in Rutland, central England, to present its offering to a highly specialized audience. At that showcase, where destinations from five continents compete, Motril defends an argument difficult to match: a highly biodiverse coastal wetland located just minutes from the urban center, with free and open access, and with observation infrastructure adapted to different levels of experience.

The economic impact of this tourism extends beyond the Charca itself. Birdwatchers staying overnight in Motril spend money in the municipality's hotels and hostels, have breakfast in downtown cafés, buy maps and field guides in local bookshops, and in many cases combine birdwatching with visits to other tourist resources in the region, such as the beaches, tropical crops, or the historic heritage of the old town. This ability to diversify spending and distribute it across different sectors makes birdwatching tourism a more resilient economic engine than other models based exclusively on sun and beach.

The birdwatching visitor profile also offers a significant seasonal advantage. While coastal tourism is concentrated in the summer months, birdwatching reaches its peak during the spring and autumn migratory passages, as well as during the winter months, when European waterbirds seek refuge in more temperate latitudes. This temporal distribution allows hospitality establishments and tourist services to maintain activity during periods that traditionally recorded very low occupancy, generating stable employment and reducing the seasonality that weighs down a large part of the sector on the Granada coast.

Collaboration between the local administration and the business community has proven key to consolidating this dynamic. The specialized agencies operating at the wetland offer guided tours in several languages, bird identification workshops, and photography routes that attract an increasingly broad audience. The Interpretation Center, recently inaugurated, functions as a meeting point and information hub, providing visitors with educational materials, recommendations on the best times for observation, and updated data on the species present at each time of year.

Data from the University of Granada points to even greater growth potential. If the average daily expenditure is maintained and the number of visitors continues the upward trend of recent years, birdwatching tourism could exceed one and a half million euros per year in direct impact on the Motril economy in the near future. That projection, together with the upcoming declaration of the Charca as a Special Protection Area for Birds, reinforces the idea that environmental conservation and economic development are not conflicting objectives, but rather pieces of the same machinery that Motril has begun to set in motion with tangible results.
